system: You are a security investigator reviewing an alert. Base every claim only on the evidence available to you. Cite the record IDs that support each observation.

supporting_observations.claim: Two failed network logons for leo.martins from 203.0.113.250 were followed about a minute later by a successful network logon for the same account from that same address.

The successful logon recorded on the domain controller used Kerberos and LogonType 3; the source address shown is 203.0.113.250, not the internal 10.40.10.23 address seen in later workstation authentication records.
The address 203.0.113.250 is in a documentation-only IP range, so these records do not establish the real-world origin or attribution of the authentication.
At 13:49, leo.martins had a local interactive logon on WS-LMARTINS-01 followed by the ordinary winlogon, userinit, and explorer process chain at medium integrity.

In that workstation session, PowerShell launched node.exe to run webpack in a clinical-portal source directory; the recorded command lines do not show an obviously malicious command, but do not establish what the PowerShell session did beyond the logged process creation.

Dropbox started at user logon and loaded a validly signed Dropbox module. Dropbox is not among the organization's approved services, but these records alone do not show syncing, data transfer, or malicious use.

The proxy recorded a successful HTTPS tunnel from leo.martins's workstation to ca.slack-edge.com; Slack is not among the organization's approved services, but the record does not reveal tunnel contents.

A network logon to WS-LMARTINS-01 as leo.martins came from WS-SOKAFOR-01, with Kerberos ticket activity from 10.40.10.23 shortly beforehand. The inventory identifies WS-SOKAFOR-01 as the IT administrator's workstation, but the records do not identify the person or process responsible for this session.

known_telemetry_limitations: The supplied records do not identify who initiated the successful network logon from 203.0.113.250 or whether that address represents the actual originating system.
The supplied workstation process records do not show the content or effects of the PowerShell session.
The Dropbox and proxy records do not provide file-sync details, transferred data, or the contents of the Slack tunnel.
The supplied records do not link the successful domain-controller logon from 203.0.113.250 to the later local workstation session or to the network logon from WS-SOKAFOR-01.
claims_not_established: That an external attacker obtained or used leo.martins's credentials.
That the successful logon from 203.0.113.250 originated outside the organization; the recorded address is in a documentation-only range.
That Dropbox or Slack was used to transfer organizational data.
That the network logon from WS-SOKAFOR-01 was authorized IT work or unauthorized access.
That the observed PowerShell, webpack, or other activity was malicious.
additional_evidence_needed: Verify whether 203.0.113.250 is a sanitized or otherwise expected address in the logging pipeline, and obtain the original network source, firewall, and routing records for the authentication.

Review surrounding domain-controller authentication events and available identity-provider or account-protection telemetry for leo.martins, including any account lockouts, password changes, or related logons.
Correlate WS-SOKAFOR-01 endpoint and remote-administration records with the 13:51 network logon to determine the initiating user, process, and purpose.
Review endpoint telemetry for the complete PowerShell command history and script content, and inspect Dropbox activity and relevant file-access or data-transfer logs.
Confirm with leo.martins and IT whether the workstation activity, Dropbox use, Slack connection, and network logon were expected or had an approved exception.
